teaching_moment_lands: REVISE (no check_strategy_tie_in rule_index — per template, recorded here not as a ledger row). Named teaching moment: naming 'compound engineering' onto the four-move loop (orient/fix/compound/close) the student just ran. Two things changed together in today's commit (eaae8cd, same commit touching both files) that weaken this specific beat. (1) compound-and-close.md's own student-facing lead-in ('The point:', line 9) now reads 'the compound step closes Kieran Klaassen's loop: ideate -> brainstorm -> plan -> work -> review -> polish -> compound -> repeat' -- Klaassen's name and the exact eight-token sequence this lecture later repeats, verbatim, printed BEFORE the retro prompt runs. By the time the student reaches 'The pattern has a name. Kieran Klaassen at Every calls it compound engineering,' they already have the name; the sentence is staged as a reveal but functions as a rerun of something Ex3's body told them roughly twenty minutes earlier. This also makes the lecture's own maintainer claim ('Klaassen is named once on the student surface. The cap is deliberate.') currently false -- he is named in two files, with the fuller citation now identical between them. (2) The specific mapping asked about: 'That is the orient, fix, compound, close loop cut at different joints; the names differ, the loop doesn't' sits one sentence after an eight-arrow chain, describing a four-move loop as the 'same loop' as an eight-move one on the strength of one anchored correspondence (retro = his 'compound', step seven of eight). The anchor is precise and holds. The larger claim is asserted, not shown -- 'the names differ' is narrower than what actually happened (a granularity change, not a relabeling), and the sentence doesn't say where the other three of the student's four moves land inside the other seven of Klaassen's eight. Reasonable-persona-variation test: a numerically-attentive engineer reader (a normal member of this specific audience) notices the 4-vs-8 mismatch sitting directly beside a claim that only 'names' moved, and the beat asks them to take that on faith at the exact moment it is supposed to feel self-evident. Neither problem is catastrophic -- the training-construction story around it (bulletpoints -> wrong prototypes -> rules -> agents checking agents) still lands cleanly and the single anchored correspondence is genuinely accurate -- but together they mean the specific 'same loop, different joints' beat this lecture closes on is thinner than the file currently presents it as being.
